name: Yusuf Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Yusuf, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we don't sell anything. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an injection moulding operator at Kestrel Automotive, we make plastic parts for cars: door trim clips, vent grilles, little things nobody notices until they rattle. Plastic pellets go into a heated barrel, get squeezed into a steel mould at huge pressure, and out comes a part every twenty-eight seconds. I watch three presses, pull samples, check them against the drawings, clear short shots, which is when the mould doesn't fill properly. Eleven months in, and I still need the setter, Paolo, when a mould needs changing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving things. When a press starts throwing out parts with flash, thin plastic leaking at the edges, I take a photo of the settings screen and ask an AI app what might cause it, then I go and argue with Paolo about it. He hates that and he loves it. What wears me out is the smell of hot plastic in summer and the twelve-hour weekend shifts, which pay well but mean I miss Mira's swimming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, I'm a bit disappointed. Everybody kept promising the future, and we got a slightly better spell checker. At work I'd joke with Paolo that his job is safe so he can stop pretending to be scared of my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've got to get good the old way, which is fine. I'd want to become a setter, the person who changes and tunes the moulds. That's two or three years of learning from Paolo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd ask Kestrel for the setter training and keep using AI tools on his phone to understand faults faster. He'd stay active in the union and push for a better weekend premium. He'd put the extra pay from becoming a setter into the children's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. I like change, so a world that stays the same is not my favourite picture, but it's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the AI app at work. Does your company know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor knows and pretends not to. There's no rule against it, but there's no rule for it either. I never put anything secret in, just the settings on the screen and what the part looks like. If anything, I'd like the union to write a proper rule, so people aren't scared of using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to learn the setter's job if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely. I came to the factory at forty-two after fifteen years as a delivery driver, and I don't want to be the guy who just pulls parts until he's sixty. Setters get paid more and they get to think. That's the bit I want.

S0.say: I'm honestly a bit disappointed: everybody promised the future and we got a slightly better spell checker. At work I'd tell Paolo his job is safe so he can stop pretending to be scared of my phone.
S0.think: It means I have to get good the old way, which is fine with me. I'd want to become a setter, which is two or three years of learning from Paolo.
S0.do: Asks Kestrel for setter training and keeps using AI on his phone to understand faults faster. Pushes the union for a better weekend premium and a clear rule on using AI tools, and puts the extra setter pay into the children's savings.
S0.feel: Calm and a little bored, because he enjoys change.
S0.quote: Everybody kept promising the future, and we got a slightly better spell checker.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is the rare operator who is disappointed that nothing changes. He already uses AI daily on the shop floor, quietly and without a rule either way, and wants the union to write one. His ambition is clear: he wants to become a setter so he gets to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if the workers get a share. Faster machines, fewer injuries, but the time saved should come back to us as shorter weeks, not as fewer of us. I'd post that on the union group and I'd say it to the managers' faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. Most of my job is the boring part, and I'd be happy to hand it over. The people who'll struggle are the ones who've done one press for twenty years and hate screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd volunteer for the first robot cell Kestrel puts in and ask to be trained as a cobot technician, cobots being robot arms built to work next to people. He'd take an evening course in basic robot programming in the first year, about eight hundred on his own money if the company won't pay. He'd push the union to make training paid and open to everyone, not just the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. I'd feel like the world was finally moving at my speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people who'll struggle are the twenty-year press people. Is there someone specific?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Sandra on the night shift. She's brilliant on the presses but she still prints her emails. I'd want to sit with her on the new kit, the way Paolo sits with me on the moulds. Fair's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Eight hundred on your own money. How does your partner feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aylin's a pharmacist, she'd say do it, she's the one who told me to leave delivery driving. We have savings and we rent out the downstairs flat, so eight hundred isn't scary. What's scary to her is me getting bored. She's seen what that does.

S1.say: This is good if the workers get a share: the time saved should come back as shorter weeks, not as fewer of us. I'd post that on the union group and say it to the managers' faces.
S1.think: I'd do well out of it, because most of my job is the boring part and I'd happily hand it over. The ones who'll struggle are people who've done one press for twenty years and hate screens.
S1.do: Volunteers for Kestrel's first robot cell and asks to train as a cobot technician. Pays about eight hundred for an evening robot programming course in the first year if the company won't, and pushes the union to make training paid and open to all.
S1.feel: Calm and even excited, as if the world is finally moving at his speed.
S1.quote: I'd feel like the world was finally moving at my speed.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption looks like an opportunity to Yusuf, and his savings and rental flat make the risk feel small. His progressive views show up as wanting gains shared through shorter weeks. He wants to pass on to older colleagues the help he's had, a sign of real solidarity rather than just a slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest decision any government will make, and they need to make it in months. Everyone gets a basic income, robots get taxed, and the factories that save fortunes pay into it. I'd be out on the streets for that and I'd post about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for once I wouldn't know what to learn. My whole plan is learn the next thing before everyone else. If the AI can learn the next thing faster than me, being quick doesn't help. That's a strange feeling for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd still get into the robot cell in the first months, because someone has to install and watch the robots while they come in. He'd join the campaign for a basic income and a robot tax and stand for a union rep position. He and Aylin would stop the loft conversion and keep the rental flat as a steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me as much, for the whole thing. It's like being on a bus that's going too fast even if you've got a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said before you'd do well. Is that still true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a year or two. Somebody has to plug the robots in and tell the bosses why they don't work. But Aylin's job is on the list too, AI can check prescriptions, and then the two of us are holding the same umbrella. I don't think being early saves you if the wave is big enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do now, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use AI even more, every day, so I understand what it can and can't do. Get my name known as the robot guy at Kestrel. And talk to the kids, Deniz especially, he's eleven and thinks he'll be a footballer, which might be the safest plan of all of us.

S2.say: This is the biggest decision any government will make, and they have months to make it: a basic income for everyone and a tax on robots paid by the factories saving fortunes. I'd be out on the streets for it and post about it every day.
S2.think: For once I wouldn't know what to learn, because my whole plan is to learn the next thing first. If the AI learns faster than me, being quick doesn't help.
S2.do: Gets into Kestrel's robot cell in the first months to help install and watch the robots, and stands for union rep. Joins the campaign for a basic income and robot tax, and with Aylin cancels the loft conversion while keeping the rental flat as steady income.
S2.feel: Anxious, more for society than himself, like being on a bus that's going too fast even with a seat.
S2.quote: I don't think being early saves you if the wave is big enough.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture shakes Yusuf's core strategy of staying a step ahead, and he notices that himself. His partner's job being exposed too worries him more than his own. He still acts fast, but his energy goes into politics and collective demands as much as personal advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd say, let's plan this together, properly: retraining funds, shorter weeks, a public share in the robot companies. I'd say it at work and at union conferences, and I'd say it hopefully, not angrily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is my kind of timeline. I could be a qualified robot technician by year two and leading a cell by year four. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd be in the room where things get decided, not outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd start a two-year part-time mechatronics diploma, which mixes mechanics, electronics and programming, in the first year, with Kestrel paying half if the union wins it. He'd push for a robot transition agreement at the plant and help older workers like Sandra into the new roles. He'd use some savings to buy shares in a robotics fund, which he admits feels odd for a left-wing guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a lively way. There's worry, but there's a plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying shares in robot companies. You said that feels odd. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the robots are going to own everything, I want my kids to own a slice of the robots. I'd rather the government did that for everyone, a public fund, and I'd vote for it. Until they do, I'll do it for my family and feel a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes, for you, between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'm running behind the wave. In five I can paddle out to meet it. That's the difference, and it's huge for someone like me who moves quickly anyway.

S3.say: Let's plan this together, properly, with retraining funds, shorter weeks and a public share in the robot companies. I'd say it at work and at union conferences, hopefully rather than angrily.
S3.think: Five years is my kind of timeline: qualified robot technician by year two, leading a cell by year four. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd be in the room where things get decided.
S3.do: Starts a two-year part-time mechatronics diploma in the first year, pushing for Kestrel to pay half, and helps older workers into new roles. Buys shares in a robotics fund with some savings and campaigns for a robot transition agreement at the plant.
S3.feel: Uneasy but energised, with worry alongside a plan.
S3.quote: If the robots are going to own everything, I want my kids to own a slice of the robots.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Yusuf's way of working, and he immediately maps out a career path. He's candid about the tension between his left-wing politics and buying robotics shares, and resolves it as a stopgap until a public fund exists. The paddling-out image shows how much the extra warning matters to someone who acts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right, so let's not waste it on arguing whether it's coming. Four-day weeks first, then three, with the same pay. I'd say people like me should help build it, not just watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd be fifty-three with skills that didn't exist when I started, a paid house and a rental flat. The danger for me is getting comfortable and forgetting the people on the night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd finish the mechatronics diploma by year three and move up to cell lead or into Kestrel's maintenance team. He'd keep investing a small amount monthly in the robotics fund and pay off the mortgage by about 2032. He'd stay a union rep and help run training sessions for older workers in AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Hopeful, even. A decade is a long time to get ready if you start on the first day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is also a long time to put things off. Would you start straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start next week. That's just who I am, I bought a phone with a touchscreen before anyone in my street. The risk for me isn't starting late, it's starting three different things and finishing none. Aylin would keep me honest on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about the world they'd grow up into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Deniz and Mira to learn how to learn, and to be kind, because a world full of robots needs people who look after each other. And I'd tell them their dad started in a factory at forty-two and ended up teaching robots. That's a good story for a kid.

S4.say: Ten years is a real chance to get this right, so let's not waste it arguing whether it's coming. Four-day weeks first, then three, on the same pay, and people like me should help build it.
S4.think: I'd be fine, maybe better than fine: fifty-three, with new skills, a paid-off house and a rental flat. The danger is getting comfortable and forgetting the people on the night shift.
S4.do: Finishes the mechatronics diploma by year three and moves up to cell lead or maintenance at Kestrel. Keeps investing monthly in a robotics fund, pays off the mortgage by about 2032, and runs AI tool training for older workers as union rep.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, because a decade is plenty of time if he starts on day one.
S4.quote: The risk for me isn't starting late, it's starting three different things and finishing none.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Yusuf is calm and even hopeful, and his self-awareness stands out: his real risk is scattered effort, not inaction. His wealth and adaptability make him confident, but he keeps returning to colleagues who might be left behind. He tells his own story as one he'd be proud to pass on to his children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of me, I'd find something, but because Aylin's job and mine and everyone's goes at once, and governments can't move that fast. What would help is a basic income switched on quickly and a public share in the companies building the robots, so the money doesn't all end up with a few people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd actually want the robots. I would, if they did the hot, boring, dangerous bits and we got the time back. Paolo's got a bad shoulder from twenty years of lifting moulds. If a robot saves the next Paolo's shoulder, I'm for it, as long as the next Paolo still gets paid.

headlineQuote: If a robot saves the next Paolo's shoulder, I'm for it, as long as the next Paolo still gets paid.
portrait: Yusuf Fischer is 43, a former delivery driver who has spent eleven months as an injection moulding operator at Kestrel Automotive and is still learning from the setter, Paolo. He uses AI tools every day on the shop floor, has a pharmacist partner, Aylin, two children, strong savings and a rented-out downstairs flat. He's left-wing and union-minded, but he also moves first and enjoys change. He's calm or even excited in the milder pictures and when AGI is ten years off, uneasy with five, and anxious with two, mostly for his partner and for society, putting his energy into retraining, a robot tax, a basic income and helping older colleagues.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his job, Aylin's and everyone else's would go at once and governments can't move that fast.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income switched on quickly and a public share in the companies building the robots, so the money doesn't end up with a few people.
